## Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosures (Edge AI / NPU Silicon, MITRE CVE Candidates)
- **CAN-2026-2038801 (GitHub Issue #75 / NGZA-AX-LLM #1)**: Unauthenticated OS Command Injection in Audio Preprocessing in AXERA-TECH AX-LLM (`src/runner/utils/audio_processor.cpp` / `AudioWrapper.hpp`, CVSS 8.4 High)
- **CAN-2026-2038776 (GitHub Issue #76 / NGZA-AX-LLM #2)**: Out-of-Bounds Read + Integer Truncation in Prompt Prefill & CMM DMA Mask in AXERA-TECH AX-LLM (`src/runner/LLM.hpp`, CVSS 7.5 High)
- **CAN-2026-2038802 (GitHub Issue #77 / NGZA-AX-LLM #3)**: NULL Pointer Dereference & Out-of-Bounds Read in Token Streaming Callback in AXERA-TECH AX-LLM (`src/main_api.cpp`, CVSS 7.5 High)
- **CAN-2026-2034987 (GitHub Issue #80 / NGZA-AX-LLM #4)**: Stack-Based Buffer Overflow in Layer Filename Formatting in AXERA-TECH AX-LLM (`src/runner/LLM.hpp`, CVSS 7.8 High)
- **CAN-2026-2038777 (GitHub Issue #81 / NGZA-AX-LLM #5)**: Heap Out-of-Bounds Write in Multimodal RoPE Position Indexing in AXERA-TECH AX-LLM (`src/runner/LLM.hpp`, CVSS 8.1 High)
- **CAN-2026-2038778 (GitHub Issue #82 / NGZA-AX-LLM #6)**: Integer Overflow in Multimodal Vision Preprocessing in AXERA-TECH AX-LLM (`src/runner/utils/image_processor.cpp`, CVSS 7.5 High)
- **CAN-2026-2038779 (NGZA-AX-LLM #7)**: Double-Free & Use-After-Free in CLI Argument Error Handling in AXERA-TECH AX-LLM (`src/cmdline.hpp`, CVSS 7.3 High)

![Hunting Edge AI CVEs Banner](../assets/hunting_edge_ai_cves.png)

> **Companion Architectural Advisory:** This post is our hands-on hardware lab diary and exploit reproduction walkthrough. For the enterprise supply-chain analysis and memory boundary architecture breakdown, read my official advisory on the Cobalt blog: **[Dissecting the AX-LLM CVEs: Why Edge AI Memory and Execution Boundaries Matter](https://www.cobalt.io/blog/dissecting-the-ax-llm-cves-why-edge-ai-memory-and-execution-boundaries-matter)**.

## Why Our Hardware Lab Looked Past the Prompt

If you read our earlier guides on [Taming the Axera AX8850 Edge NPU](taming-ax8850-edge-npu.html) and [Zero-Copy NPU Memory Pipelines](ultimate-guide-zero-copy-ax8850.html), you know how we wired a 24 TOPS PCIe NPU card into `NextGenPVE`. Once we got Qwen2.5 and DeepSeek models screaming at the silicon layer inside `LXC 211`, my red team instincts kicked in.

Everyone in offensive AI talks about prompt injection. Security conferences run endless tracks on jailbreaks, system prompt extraction, and guardrail bypasses. Those bugs matter, sure.

Below the prompt sits a much nastier attack surface. On edge AI hardware, your JSON payload does not stay inside a memory-safe Python sandbox in a hyperscale cloud. A lightweight C++ HTTP wrapper parses that JSON and hands raw pointers straight to `/dev/ax_npu` over Contiguous Media Memory (CMM) Direct Memory Access (DMA) channels.

We decided to audit the open-source `AXERA-TECH/ax-llm` C++ inference engine running on our physical **Radxa AI Core AX-M1** (`ax650_card_v1.0` / Axera AX8850) testbed. By pairing fast command-line source code triage with live AddressSanitizer (ASan) and hardware DMA fault checks, we uncovered **seven distinct vulnerabilities** across the runtime. All seven flaws have been cataloged with MITRE under official CVE Candidate (`CAN-2026-*`) identifiers while final CVE publication is pending.

---

## The Vulnerability Scorecard

Before we walk through the terminal harnesses and GDB traces, here is the full breakdown of what we found inside `AXERA-TECH/ax-llm` (`commit a0fb3f2` / v0.1.0). All seven vulnerabilities were reported to **AXERA-TECH** and assigned official **MITRE CVE Candidate (`CAN`)** identifiers pending final publication:

| MITRE Candidate / Tracking | Vulnerability Class | Location | Severity |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **CAN-2026-2038776** ([Issue #76](https://github.com/AXERA-TECH/ax-llm/issues/76)) | Out-of-Bounds Read + Integer Truncation in Prompt Prefill & DMA Mask | `src/runner/LLM.hpp` | **7.5 (High)** |
| **CAN-2026-2034987** ([Issue #80](https://github.com/AXERA-TECH/ax-llm/issues/80)) | Stack-Based Buffer Overflow in Layer Filename Formatting | `src/runner/LLM.hpp` | **7.8 (High)** |
| **CAN-2026-2038777** ([Issue #81](https://github.com/AXERA-TECH/ax-llm/issues/81)) | Heap Out-of-Bounds Write in Multimodal RoPE Position Indexing | `src/runner/LLM.hpp` | **8.1 (High)** |
| **CAN-2026-2038778** ([Issue #82](https://github.com/AXERA-TECH/ax-llm/issues/82)) | Integer Overflow in Multimodal Vision Preprocessing | `src/runner/utils/image_processor.cpp` | **7.5 (High)** |
| **CAN-2026-2038779** (`NGZA-AX-LLM #7`) | Double-Free & Use-After-Free in CLI Argument Error Handling | `src/cmdline.hpp` | **7.3 (High)** |
| **CAN-2026-2038801** ([Issue #75](https://github.com/AXERA-TECH/ax-llm/issues/75)) | Unauthenticated OS Command Injection in Audio Preprocessing | `src/runner/AudioWrapper.hpp` | **8.4 / 9.8 (Critical)** |
| **CAN-2026-2038802** ([Issue #77](https://github.com/AXERA-TECH/ax-llm/issues/77)) | Heap Out-of-Bounds Read & NULL Dereference in Token Streaming Callback | `src/main_api.cpp` | **7.5 (High)** |

You can read the broader industry context and why edge AI memory boundaries fail in my companion piece on Cobalt: [Dissecting the AX-LLM CVEs: Why Edge AI Memory and Execution Boundaries Matter](https://www.cobalt.io/blog/dissecting-the-ax-llm-cves-why-edge-ai-memory-and-execution-boundaries-matter). Down below, we are going straight into the lab methodology and the exact C++ code paths.

---

## How I Hunt C++ Silicon Bugs by Ear at 500 WPM

People ask how a blind hacker audits low-level C++ NPU drivers and memory allocators. Honestly, as I broke down in [Hacking by Ear at 500 WPM](hacking-by-ear-at-500-wpm-screen-readers.html), [Why I Use AI to Build Accessible CLIs and PWAs](why-i-use-ai-to-build-accessible-clis-and-pwas.html), and my [Hacking While Blind CLI Survival Guide on TheBlindHacker.com](https://theblindhacker.com/hackingwhileblind), a screen reader running at 500 words per minute is an unfair advantage for source code auditing.

Sighted engineers often skim C++ files visually. Their eyes jump over boilerplate `sprintf` calls, implicit `int` casts, or missing bounds checks because the code *looks* well-formatted. When you listen to code through a CLI pipeline using `ripgrep`, `awk`, and `sed`, every single type cast and pointer arithmetic operation hits your ears in strict sequence.

We call our workflow **SRC + EER**: **Source Code Review** paired with **Edge Execution Review**.

### Step 1: The Two-Step Triage Rule

Most vendor edge AI SDKs start life as quick board-support demo code (`ax-samples`). Later, downstream OEMs wrap that exact same C++ code inside `cpp-httplib` and ship it as an OpenAI-compatible `/v1/chat/completions` daemon running as `root`.

When I audit an embedded AI repo from the command line, I run a two-step filter:

1. **Trace Untrusted Network or Config Inputs:** Find every place where an HTTP JSON field, an image header, an audio path, or a model config enters the binary.
2. **Check the Memory Sink Before the Hardware Call:** Verify whether that input touches `sprintf`, `std::system`, `memcpy`, or a hardware DMA transfer (`ax_engine_run_group` / `ax_cmm_alloc`) before a hard clamp checks its size.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Untrusted Input (JSON / Image / Audio / Config)"] --> B{"Input Boundary Check?"}
    B -- "Missing Clamp" --> C["Host Heap / Stack Buffer"]
    B -- "Unquoted Shell String" --> D["std::system() Execution"]
    C --> E["CMM Physical DMA Transfer (/dev/ax_npu)"]
    E --> F["NPU Fault / Token Corruption / Crash"]
    D --> G["Root RCE on Edge Device"]
```

### Step 2: Fast CLI Grep Sweeps

Before we even fire up the ARM64 compiler on the Radxa board, we sweep the repository for classic C/C++ footguns. Here is the exact command set we ran against `ax-llm`:

```bash
# 1. Hunt unbounded string formatting and raw shell calls
grep -rnE "sprintf\(|vsprintf\(|strcpy\(|strcat\(|system\(|popen\(" src/

# 2. Hunt raw memory copies and CMM/DMA buffer operations
grep -rnE "memcpy\(|memset\(|ax_cmm_|llm_Embed\(|p_vir_addr" src/

# 3. Hunt narrow integer casts near vector allocations
grep -rnE "static_cast<int>|unsigned short|\.resize\(" src/
```

That three-minute sweep lit up the terminal like a Christmas tree. Reading the grep output is only half the job, though. To prove real impact on an embedded NPU, you have to run the binary on the silicon and watch what breaks.

---

## Lab Walkthrough: Reproducing All Seven Flaws on the AX8850

We mounted our Radxa AI Core AX-M1 inside our `NextGenPVE` host and passed the `/dev/ax_*` device nodes into our test environment. We built two versions of the `ax-llm` binary on `aarch64`: a standard release build linked against the hardware NPU drivers, and an instrumented debug build compiled with `-fsanitize=address,undefined -g -O1`.

Here is how each bug works under the hood, what we saw on the hardware, and how to fix it.

---

### 1. CAN-2026-2038776: Out-of-Bounds Read + Integer Truncation in Prompt Prefill & DMA Mask

* **Location:** `src/runner/LLM.hpp` (Lines 523 and 592) | **GitHub Issue:** [#76](https://github.com/AXERA-TECH/ax-llm/issues/76)
* **CVSS v3.1:** 7.5 (High)

In `LLM.hpp`, the prompt prefill handler accepts a `std::vector<int> &_token_ids` array directly from the tokenizer. The engine allocates a fixed Contiguous Media Memory (CMM) physical buffer for the NPU context window (`attr.max_token_len`, typically 1024 or 2048 tokens).

Look at what happens when a user sends a prompt that exceeds `max_token_len`:

```cpp
// Vulnerable Code (src/runner/LLM.hpp)
int token_len = (int)_token_ids.size(); // [1] Unchecked input size!

// Line 523: Unbounded read/write past pre-allocated embed_selector buffer
for (int i = 0; i < token_len; i++) {
    embed_selector.Embed(_token_ids[i], p_embed + i * attr.tokens_embed_size);
}

// Line 592: 16-bit integer truncation in attention mask setup
unsigned short mask_val = (unsigned short)(token_len * attr.kv_cache_size);
memcpy(cmm_mask_vir_addr, src_mask, token_len * attr.tokens_embed_size); // [2] DMA buffer overflow!
```

We tracked down two bugs right next to each other here. First, `token_len` never checks against `attr.max_token_len` before indexing into `p_embed` and copying data into the NPU CMM buffer. Second, casting `token_len * attr.kv_cache_size` to a 16-bit `unsigned short` wraps around modularly once the product passes `65,535`.

**What Happened on the Silicon:**
We sent an unauthenticated HTTP `POST` request to `/v1/chat/completions` containing 4,096 tokens on a model configured for `max_token_len = 1024`. The `memcpy` into `cmm_mask_vir_addr` read past the host heap vector and smashed adjacent CMM physical memory pages.

On our live Qwen2.5-7B NPU instance, the attack did not always trigger a clean Linux `SIGSEGV` right away. When a prompt overflowed the attention mask by just a few hundred tokens, it corrupted the NPU KV-cache weights in place. The token sampler lost its mind and streamed endless lines of raw Chinese Mojibake (`烫烫烫...` and `锟斤拷...`). Those characters come from the classic C++ uninitialized heap and stack byte patterns `0xCCCC` and `0xCDCD` decoded as UTF-8, right before the `/dev/ax_npu` kernel driver locked up the inference queue.

**The Fix:**
Clamp `_token_ids.size()` against `attr.max_token_len` before touching any embedding or CMM buffers, and replace `unsigned short` with `size_t`.

```cpp
// Fixed Code
if (_token_ids.empty() || _token_ids.size() > static_cast<size_t>(attr.max_token_len)) {
    ALOGE("Input token length (%zu) exceeds NPU max_token_len (%d)", _token_ids.size(), attr.max_token_len);
    return -1;
}
size_t token_len = _token_ids.size();
size_t mask_bytes = token_len * static_cast<size_t>(attr.tokens_embed_size);
```

---

### 2. CAN-2026-2034987: Stack-Based Buffer Overflow in Layer Filename Formatting

* **Location:** `src/runner/LLM.hpp` (Line 235) | **GitHub Issue:** [#80](https://github.com/AXERA-TECH/ax-llm/issues/80)
* **CVSS v3.1:** 7.8 (High)

When the engine boots up, it loads split `.axmodel` NPU weight shards from disk using a filename template stored in the model JSON config (`filename_llm_axmodel`).

```cpp
// Vulnerable Code (src/runner/LLM.hpp, Line 235)
char filename[128]; // Fixed 128-byte stack buffer
for (int i = 0; i < attr.axmodel_num; i++) {
    sprintf(filename, attr.filename_llm_axmodel.c_str(), i); // Unbounded sprintf!
    load_axmodel(filename, i);
}
```

Our initial `grep` for `sprintf(` flagged line 235 immediately. A 128-byte stack buffer holds the path, and `sprintf` formats a user-controlled `std::string` right into it without checking the length. Even a deep directory path on a Linux filesystem can blow past 128 characters.

**What Happened on the Silicon:**
We crafted a configuration file (`malicious_template_config.json`) where `filename_llm_axmodel` held 256 `"A"` characters followed by `%d.axmodel`. Running `./build/ax_llm_runner --config malicious_template_config.json` smashed the stack frame on the spot. On our standard release build, the binary crashed with a `stack smashing detected (SIGABRT)` fault. On our ASan build, it threw `ERROR: AddressSanitizer: stack-buffer-overflow on address ... WRITE of size 266`.

**The Fix:**
Replace `sprintf` with `snprintf` and increase the path buffer to `PATH_MAX` (or `512` bytes), checking for truncation before loading the shard.

```cpp
// Fixed Code
char filename[512];
int written = snprintf(filename, sizeof(filename), attr.filename_llm_axmodel.c_str(), i);
if (written < 0 || static_cast<size_t>(written) >= sizeof(filename)) {
    ALOGE("Model path template exceeds buffer bounds");
    return -1;
}
```

---

### 3. CAN-2026-2038777: Heap Out-of-Bounds Write in Multimodal RoPE Indexing

* **Location:** `src/runner/LLM.hpp` (Lines 422 to 450) | **GitHub Issue:** [#81](https://github.com/AXERA-TECH/ax-llm/issues/81)
* **CVSS v3.1:** 8.1 (High)

Vision-Language Models (VLMs) like Qwen2-VL use 3D Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) to map image patches and text tokens into a shared coordinate space. Let's look at how `LLM.hpp` calculates those RoPE indices:

```cpp
// Vulnerable Code (src/runner/LLM.hpp, Lines 422-450)
std::vector<int> position_ids(attr.max_token_len * 3); // Pre-allocated for max_token_len
int idx = 0;
for (size_t i = 0; i < _token_ids.size(); i++) {
    if (_token_ids[i] == IMAGE_CONTEXT_TOKEN) {
        for (int h = 0; h < img_grid_h; h++) {
            for (int w = 0; w < img_grid_w; w++) {
                // Unchecked write into position_ids!
                position_ids[idx++] = current_pos;
                position_ids[idx++] = h;
                position_ids[idx++] = w;
            }
        }
    }
}
```

The vector `position_ids` allocates `attr.max_token_len * 3` integers up front. Inside the nested loop, `idx` increments on every image patch and token without ever checking if `idx + 2 < position_ids.size()`.

**What Happened on the Silicon:**
We fed the multimodal runner a prompt packed with repeated `IMAGE_CONTEXT_TOKEN` markers alongside high-resolution grid dimensions (`img_grid_h = 64, img_grid_w = 64`). That single image grid writes `64 * 64 * 3 = 12,288` integers into a vector sized for only `3,072` integers.

The loop wrote 32-bit position integers right past the end of `position_ids` into adjacent `std::allocator` heap metadata and C++ object vtables. Under GDB and ASan on our ARM64 node, the binary died immediately with `AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow WRITE of size 4 at 0xffff... in LLM::generate_rope_ids()`.

**The Fix:**
Verify that `idx + 3 <= position_ids.size()` on every iteration of the RoPE generator loop.

```cpp
// Fixed Code
if (static_cast<size_t>(idx + 3) > position_ids.size()) {
    ALOGE("RoPE position index overflow: idx=%d exceeds capacity=%zu", idx, position_ids.size());
    return -1;
}
```

---

### 4. CAN-2026-2038778: Integer Overflow in Multimodal Vision Preprocessing

* **Location:** `src/runner/utils/image_processor.cpp` (Lines 45 to 78) | **GitHub Issue:** [#82](https://github.com/AXERA-TECH/ax-llm/issues/82)
* **CVSS v3.1:** 7.5 (High)

Before the NPU encodes an image, `image_processor.cpp` resizes and normalizes the RGB pixel buffer. Look at the arithmetic used to allocate the target `std::vector<float>` buffer:

```cpp
// Vulnerable Code (src/runner/utils/image_processor.cpp, Lines 45-78)
int target_h = img_height * scale_factor;
int target_w = img_width * scale_factor;
int total_pixels = target_h * target_w * 3; // [1] 32-bit signed integer overflow!

std::vector<float> resized_buf(total_pixels); // [2] Sign-extended to huge size_t or tiny wrap!
for (int y = 0; y < target_h; y++) {
    for (int x = 0; x < target_w; x++) {
        resized_buf[(y * target_w + x) * 3] = ...; // [3] Out-of-bounds heap write!
    }
}
```

The math uses 32-bit signed `int` variables. If `target_h * target_w * 3` exceeds `INT_MAX` (`2,147,483,647`), signed integer overflow triggers undefined behavior in C++.

**What Happened on the Silicon:**
We tested two crafted image headers:
1. **Negative Sign-Extension Crash:** With `target_h = 30000` and `target_w = 30000`, the product `30000 * 30000 * 3` equals `2,700,000,000`. In 32-bit signed math, that wraps to `-1,594,967,296`. When `std::vector` casts that negative `int` to an unsigned 64-bit `size_t`, it asks the allocator for `18,446,744,072,114,584,320` bytes (~18.4 exabytes). The daemon crashes on the spot with an unhandled `std::bad_alloc` exception.
2. **Positive Wrap-Around Heap Corruption:** When dimensions are tuned so `target_h * target_w * 3` wraps past `2^32` into a small positive integer (for example, `4096` bytes), `resized_buf` allocates a tiny buffer on the heap. Then the nested `y` and `x` loops write millions of float values past the end of that buffer.

**The Fix:**
Perform all dimension math in `size_t` and enforce hard maximum image dimensions (such as `4096 x 4096`) before allocation.

```cpp
// Fixed Code
constexpr size_t MAX_IMG_DIM = 4096;
if (target_h <= 0 || target_w <= 0 ||
    static_cast<size_t>(target_h) > MAX_IMG_DIM ||
    static_cast<size_t>(target_w) > MAX_IMG_DIM) {
    return -1;
}
size_t total_pixels = static_cast<size_t>(target_h) * static_cast<size_t>(target_w) * 3ULL;
std::vector<float> resized_buf(total_pixels);
```

---

### 5. CAN-2026-2038779: Double-Free & Use-After-Free in CLI Argument Error Handling

* **Location:** `src/cmdline.hpp` (Lines 310 to 365) | **Tracking ID:** `NGZA-AX-LLM #7`
* **CVSS v3.1:** 7.3 (High)

In `src/cmdline.hpp`, the `cmdline::parser` class stores option objects inside a `std::map<std::string, option_base*>`. When parsing fails or an invalid flag arrives, the error cleanup path manually deletes option pointers without removing them from the map. Then the class destructor (`~parser()`) loops over that same map and calls `delete` a second time.

**What Happened on the Silicon:**
Passing a malformed flag sequence to the runner triggered the error handler, which freed the option pointers and then invoked stack unwinding. Under `glibc` on our ARM64 board, the allocator caught the corrupted fastbin/tcache list and aborted with `free(): double free detected in tcache 2 (SIGABRT)`. Under ASan, it flagged `AddressSanitizer: attempting double-free on 0x... in cmdline::parser::~parser()`.

**The Fix:**
Replace raw `option_base*` pointers in `cmdline::parser` with `std::unique_ptr<option_base>` so RAII handles memory cleanup once and only once.

---

### 6. CAN-2026-2038801: Unauthenticated OS Command Injection in Audio Preprocessing

* **Location:** `src/runner/AudioWrapper.hpp` (Lines 42 to 58) | **GitHub Issue:** [#75](https://github.com/AXERA-TECH/ax-llm/issues/75)
* **CVSS v3.1:** 8.4 / 9.8 (Critical)

This was my favorite find of the entire hardware sprint. When `ax-llm` runs in multimodal audio mode, it needs to convert incoming audio files or URLs into 16kHz mono WAV files before feeding them to the Whisper/Audio NPU encoder. How did the developer implement audio resampling in C++? Take a look:

```cpp
// Vulnerable Code (src/runner/AudioWrapper.hpp, Lines 42-58)
int preprocess_audio(const std::string &audio_path, const std::string &output_wav) {
    char cmd[512];
    snprintf(cmd, sizeof(cmd), "ffmpeg -y -i \"%s\" -ar 16000 -ac 1 \"%s\"",
             audio_path.c_str(), output_wav.c_str());
    return std::system(cmd); // Direct shell execution of user input!
}
```

There is zero sanitization on `audio_path`. The code drops the string straight between double quotes and hands it to `/bin/sh -c` via `std::system()`.

**What Happened on the Silicon:**
We passed an `audio_url` / `audio_path` value containing:

```text
test.wav"; id > /tmp/pwned; #
```

The embedded double quote closed the `-i` argument early. Next, `/bin/sh` executed `id > /tmp/pwned` with the privileges of the `ax_llm` service, and the `#` commented out the rest of the `ffmpeg` line. Because NPU access on embedded Linux boards almost always runs as `root` (to open `/dev/ax_npu` and `/dev/mem`), checking `/tmp/pwned` showed:

```text
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
```

One unauthenticated JSON request gives an attacker instant root shell execution on the edge device.

**The Fix:**
Never pass user-supplied strings to `std::system()`. Execute `ffmpeg` directly using `fork()` and `execvp()` with an explicit argument array so `/bin/sh` never interprets shell metacharacters:

```cpp
// Fixed Code (POSIX execvp without /bin/sh)
pid_t pid = fork();
if (pid == 0) {
    const char *argv[] = {
        "ffmpeg", "-y", "-i", audio_path.c_str(),
        "-ar", "16000", "-ac", "1", output_wav.c_str(), nullptr
    };
    execvp("ffmpeg", const_cast<char *const *>(argv));
    _exit(127);
}
```

---

### 7. CAN-2026-2038802: Heap Out-of-Bounds Read & NULL Dereference in Token Streaming Callback

* **Location:** `src/main_api.cpp` (Lines 78 to 88) | **GitHub Issue:** [#77](https://github.com/AXERA-TECH/ax-llm/issues/77)
* **CVSS v3.1:** 7.5 (High)

In the HTTP API server (`src/main_api.cpp`), the streaming callback `llm_running_callback` sends generated tokens back to the client over Server-Sent Events (SSE). Look at lines 78 to 88:

```cpp
// Vulnerable Code (src/main_api.cpp, Lines 78-88)
void llm_running_callback(int *p_token, int n_token, const char *p_str, float token_per_sec, void *reserve) {
    // [1] Dereferences p_token[0] BEFORE checking if p_token is null or n_token == 0!
    int first_token = p_token[0];
    if (n_token <= 0 || p_token == nullptr) {
        return;
    }
    // [2] Unchecked strlen/copy on non-null-terminated C-buffer p_str
    std::string out_str(p_str);
    send_sse_chunk(out_str);
}
```

This is a textbook check-after-use bug paired with an unterminated buffer read. The function reads `p_token[0]` on the line *before* it checks `if (n_token <= 0 || p_token == nullptr)`. Worse yet, when the tokenizer emits partial multi-byte UTF-8 sequences during high-speed streaming, `p_str` lacks a trailing null byte at the chunk boundary.

**What Happened on the Silicon:**
When an empty token batch (`n_token == 0`) or a split multi-byte UTF-8 character fired the callback under concurrent HTTP load, `std::string(p_str)` read past the end of the token chunk buffer on the heap. That leaked adjacent heap bytes directly into the caller's HTTP SSE response stream, or crashed the API daemon when `p_token` was null.

**The Fix:**
Move the null and length check to the very top of `llm_running_callback` before any pointer dereference, and construct `std::string` using an explicit byte length.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How do I check if my Axera AX8850 or AX650 device is vulnerable to the AX-LLM CVEs?
Check the git commit hash or binary build date of your `ax-llm` service (`ax_llm_runner` or `main_api`). Any deployment built from `AXERA-TECH/ax-llm` at or before commit `a0fb3f2` (v0.1.0) without the bounds-clamping and `execvp` patches detailed above is vulnerable to CAN-2026-2038776, CAN-2026-2034987, CAN-2026-2038777, CAN-2026-2038778, CAN-2026-2038779, CAN-2026-2038801, and CAN-2026-2038802.

### Why do edge NPU memory corruption bugs crash the whole Linux box instead of just one process?
Standard cloud CPU processes operate in isolated virtual memory pages. By contrast, edge NPU runtimes allocate Contiguous Media Memory (CMM) or Media Memory Zone (MMZ) physical RAM blocks shared directly with `/dev/ax_npu` via DMA. When an out-of-bounds write corrupts a CMM descriptor or DMA mask, the hardware NPU engine reads invalid physical addresses, locking up the kernel driver and requiring a hard power cycle.

### Can I run AX-LLM safely inside an unprivileged Proxmox LXC container?
Passing `/dev/ax_*` device nodes into an unprivileged LXC container (like we detailed in our [Zero-Copy AX8850 Guide](ultimate-guide-zero-copy-ax8850.html)) isolates the host filesystem, which stops an OS command injection bug from overwriting host files. However, container namespaces do not validate physical CMM DMA buffer bounds. You must still patch the C++ runtime and place an authenticating reverse proxy with strict JSON payload size limits in front of `main_api`.

### Where can I read the enterprise and supply-chain analysis of these AX-LLM CVEs?
Read my companion research article on the Cobalt blog: [Dissecting the AX-LLM CVEs: Why Edge AI Memory and Execution Boundaries Matter](https://www.cobalt.io/blog/dissecting-the-ax-llm-cves-why-edge-ai-memory-and-execution-boundaries-matter), and browse all our hardware and NPU research on [TheBlindHacker.com](https://theblindhacker.com/projects).

![Why I Use AI to Build Accessible CLIs and Progressive Web Apps](../assets/why_i_use_ai_accessible_clis_pwas.png)

In my last post, [Hacking by Ear at 500 WPM](https://nextgenredteam.com/blog/hacking-by-ear-at-500-wpm-screen-readers.html), and in my [Hacking While Blind CLI Survival Guide on TheBlindHacker.com](https://theblindhacker.com/hackingwhileblind), I broke down how combining full-time screen zoom and high-speed speech output outpaces visual IDEs. Reading text through speech synthesizers at hyper-speed while navigating with locked magnification removes visual clutter. It forces you to operate on raw structure.

Consuming tools is only half the battle. At some point, you have to build them.

Building software as a visually impaired engineer usually means fighting an uphill battle against sighted developer habits. I use screen zoom at high magnification at all times, and I listen to screen reader output constantly. Most modern enterprise web apps are an absolute dumpster fire for that workflow. Buttons are unsemantic `<div>` tags with click listeners attached. Dynamic updates happen silently in the background without ARIA alerts. Modals pop open and trap your keyboard cursor in an infinite tab loop.

I stopped waiting for corporate front-end teams to fix their software. Instead, I use artificial intelligence to build my own tools. 

I do not use AI because it writes pretty code. I use AI because models do not have eyes. When you give an LLM a strict accessibility specification, it has zero visual bias. It builds pure, semantic structure.

Here is the exact blueprint I use to architect lightning-fast command-line tools and Progressive Web Apps (PWAs) that are safe, keyboard-driven, and completely accessible by design.

---

## The Sighted Developer Blindspot

Sighted developers build interfaces for their eyes first and the document object model (DOM) second.

They inspect a component in Chrome DevTools. They see a button with rounded corners, a sleek drop shadow, and a smooth hover animation. If it looks good to their eyes, they push it to production.

```html
<!-- What a sighted developer often writes -->
<div class="submit-btn-glow" onclick="triggerScan()">
  <span class="icon-radar"></span>
  Run Offensive Scan
</div>
```

To my screen reader, that code snippet is an invisible ghost. It has no semantic role. It has no accessible name. It has no keyboard focus target. If I press the Tab key, my cursor skips right past it. If I try to activate it with the Enter or Space key, nothing happens because `<div>` elements do not listen for keyboard events by default.

Now compare that to the structural reality my screen reader needs:

```html
<!-- What an accessible architecture requires -->
<button type="button" 
        id="btn-run-scan" 
        class="submit-btn-glow" 
        aria-label="Run Offensive Scan on Target Network"
        onclick="triggerScan()">
  <span class="icon-radar" aria-hidden="true"></span>
  Run Offensive Scan
</button>
```

When you multiply this visual laziness across an entire single-page dashboard with nested tab panes, infinite scroll feeds, and unannounced AJAX requests, the interface becomes unusable. Sighted engineers spend seventy percent of their sprint tweaking CSS padding and gradient color stops. They leave accessibility as a frantic checklist item forty-eight hours before a compliance audit.

I flipped that workflow completely upside down.

---

## Why the CLI and PWA Stack Wins

When I architect an internal security tool or an offensive operations dashboard, I only build two types of interfaces:

1. **A pure Command-Line Interface (CLI):** Built for automation, terminal multiplexers (`tmux`), text streams, and keyboard pipes.
2. **A Progressive Web App (PWA):** Built for structured multi-view management, offline local caching, and instant audio telemetry.

```
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                       NextGenRedTeam Operator UI                      |
+------------------------------------+----------------------------------+
|      Command-Line Interface        |      Progressive Web App         |
|  - Raw POSIX stdout / stderr       |  - Semantic HTML5 DOM Tree       |
|  - Standard exit codes (0, 1, 2)   |  - WCAG AAA contrast and focus   |
|  - Grep, sed, and jq piping        |  - ARIA live region alerts       |
|  - Terminal bell audio telemetry   |  - Web Audio API earcons         |
|  - Headless batch execution        |  - Zero-latency Service Worker   |
+------------------------------------+----------------------------------+
```

### The Terminal Advantage
A CLI has no visual layout engine to corrupt. Data comes in through arguments, standard input (`stdin`), or configuration files. Output goes out through standard output (`stdout`) or standard error (`stderr`). 

A terminal gives me complete deterministic control. I can pipe raw output into `grep`, slice fields with `awk`, or page line-by-line using `less`.

### The Progressive Web App Advantage
When a tool needs state visualization, live target switching, or structured reporting, a desktop GUI built on Electron is usually bloated and sluggish. Electron wrappers run heavy Chromium instances that consume gigabytes of RAM and frequently drop accessibility tree hooks during DOM repaints.

A well-architected PWA (like our zero-backend [JoeBro Sobro Smart Table Controller](rescuing-abandoned-iot-joebro-sobro.html), featured on [TheBlindHacker.com Projects](https://theblindhacker.com/projects)) solves those headaches:
* **Standalone Windowing:** A PWA installs directly onto the operating system. It runs in its own window without browser toolbars, URL address bars, or extension icons that clutter the keyboard navigation tree.
* **Instant Offline Execution:** Service workers cache the application shell locally. When I launch the PWA, it loads from disk in five milliseconds. There is zero network lag to freeze the screen reader virtual cursor.
* **Native Keyboard Event Routing:** You can intercept global keybindings cleanly without fighting browser shortcut collisions.
* **Hardware-Level Audio Synthesis:** Using the Web Audio API, the app can synthesize custom audio cues (earcons) directly through the operating system soundcard.

---

## Why I Use AI as My Accessibility Compiler

People ask me how I write front-end code and user interfaces without sight. The answer is simple: I treat AI models as headless structural compilers.

```
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|                  Spec-Driven AI Architecture                |
|                                                             |
|   +-----------------------------------------------------+   |
|   | 1. Human Operator Dictates Contract & WCAG Spec    |   |
|   |    - Keyboard shortcuts, ARIA regions, exit codes   |   |
|   +--------------------------+--------------------------+   |
|                              |                              |
|                              v                              |
|   +-----------------------------------------------------+   |
|   | 2. AI Generates Semantic Tree & State Machine       |   |
|   |    - Pure HTML5 semantic elements (button, dialog)  |   |
|   |    - Predictable POSIX CLI argument parser          |   |
|   +--------------------------+--------------------------+   |
|                              |                              |
|                              v                              |
|   +-----------------------------------------------------+   |
|   | 3. Automated Pre-Flight Verification Gate           |   |
|   |    - Headless browser Axe-core accessibility scan   |   |
|   |    - Tree-Sitter AST syntax and role validation     |   |
|   +-----------------------------------------------------+   |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
```

Here is why AI models excel at accessibility when directed by an experienced operator:

### 1. Models Have No Eyes
An LLM does not get seduced by aesthetic shortcuts. If you tell an AI to build a modal window, and your system prompt specifies strict WCAG AAA guidelines, the model will not use a styled `<div>`. It will use an HTML5 `<dialog>` element. It will bind the Escape key to close the window. It will place keyboard focus onto the first active element inside the container. 

Visual bias disappears. The code is generated based on semantic rules and mathematical relationships between DOM nodes.

### 2. High-Speed Spec-Driven Development
I do not ask an AI to "make me a cool web app." That produces generic junk. 

I write an architectural contract. I specify the state machine, the expected keyboard shortcuts, the exact ARIA live region policies, and the data schema. The AI produces the deterministic boilerplate in seconds. I spend my energy on system logic and security edge cases instead of typing repetitive HTML boilerplate.

### 3. Automated Tree-Sitter and Axe Linting
Before any code touches my disk, my local automation pipeline inspects the generated output. We run headless Playwright scripts backed by Axe-core and Tree-Sitter AST parsers. 

If an AI-generated component lacks an accessible label, contains an unlinked form control, or leaves an open keyboard trap, the verification gate halts immediately. The model receives the AST error log and fixes the DOM tree before I ever review it with my screen reader.

---

## Blueprint Part 1: Bulletproof Accessible CLI Architecture

If you build command-line tools for other security professionals, accessibility must be built into the core IO pipeline.

Here are the rules I enforce on every CLI tool:
1. **Never Mix Data and Errors:** Send clean data to `stdout` and diagnostic messages or errors to `stderr`. Mixing them breaks screen reader output redirection.
2. **Support Structured Machine Output:** Always provide a `--json` or `--raw` flag so operators can pipe output without parsing human-readable tables.
3. **Deterministic Exit Codes:** Never exit with code `0` on failure. Screen readers rely on system bells and exit status codes to notify users when long scans finish.
4. **Terminal Audio Telemetry:** Use terminal bell characters (`\a` or ASCII 7) or audio beeps to signal task completion on background jobs.

Here is a Python implementation of an accessible CLI harness:

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Accessible CLI Scanner Harness
NextGenRedTeam Threat Lab Utility
Enforces clean stream separation, machine output, and audio telemetry.
"""

import sys
import json
import argparse
import time

def send_terminal_alert(success: bool = True):
    """
    Emits an audible ASCII terminal bell alert.
    Single bell for success, double bell for failure.
    """
    if success:
        sys.stderr.write("\a")
        sys.stderr.flush()
    else:
        sys.stderr.write("\a")
        sys.stderr.flush()
        time.sleep(0.15)
        sys.stderr.write("\a")
        sys.stderr.flush()

def run_scan(target: str, json_mode: bool):
    """
    Simulates an offensive security asset scan.
    """
    sys.stderr.write(f"[*] Initiating scan against target: {target}\n")
    sys.stderr.flush()

    # Simulate inspection logic
    findings = [
        {"port": 22, "service": "ssh", "state": "open"},
        {"port": 80, "service": "http", "state": "open"},
        {"port": 443, "service": "https", "state": "open"},
    ]

    if json_mode:
        # Pure machine-readable output to stdout
        payload = {
            "target": target,
            "status": "completed",
            "findings_count": len(findings),
            "findings": findings
        }
        sys.stdout.write(json.dumps(payload, indent=2) + "\n")
    else:
        # Clean text-first output for screen readers
        sys.stdout.write(f"\n--- Scan Report for {target} ---\n")
        for item in findings:
            sys.stdout.write(f"Port {item['port']}/TCP is {item['state']} ({item['service']})\n")
        sys.stdout.write(f"Total findings: {len(findings)}\n")

    sys.stdout.flush()
    send_terminal_alert(success=True)

def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        description="NextGenRedTeam Accessible Security Scanner",
        formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter
    )
    parser.add_argument("target", help="IP address or hostname to audit")
    parser.add_argument("--json", action="store_true", help="Output pure structured JSON to stdout")
    
    args = parser.parse_args()

    try:
        run_scan(args.target, args.json)
        sys.exit(0)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        sys.stderr.write("\n[!] Scan aborted by operator.\n")
        send_terminal_alert(success=False)
        sys.exit(130)
    except Exception as err:
        sys.stderr.write(f"\n[ERROR] Operational failure: {str(err)}\n")
        send_terminal_alert(success=False)
        sys.exit(1)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

---

## Blueprint Part 2: Building Progressive Web Apps for the Blind

When we build web dashboards for offensive telemetry or real-time lab monitoring, a Progressive Web App gives us complete control over the interface lifecycle.

Below are the four core modules I require AI to scaffold for every accessible PWA project.

### 1. The Global ARIA Live Region Dispatcher
Screen readers will not announce background updates unless you pipe them through an `aria-live` region. 

You need two distinct channels:
* `polite`: Waits until the screen reader finishes speaking the current sentence. Used for status changes, scan logs, and non-blocking notifications.
* `assertive`: Interrupts the speech synthesizer immediately. Used for critical errors, session expirations, and safety aborts.

```javascript
/**
 * Accessible Live Announcement Dispatcher
 * Manages polite and assertive speech output buffers.
 */
class LiveAnnouncer {
  constructor() {
    this.politeRegion = this._createRegion('live-polite', 'polite');
    this.assertiveRegion = this._createRegion('live-assertive', 'assertive');
  }

  _createRegion(id, mode) {
    let el = document.getElementById(id);
    if (!el) {
      el = document.createElement('div');
      el.id = id;
      el.setAttribute('role', 'status');
      el.setAttribute('aria-live', mode);
      el.setAttribute('aria-atomic', 'true');
      // Hide visually while keeping it readable by speech synthesizers
      Object.assign(el.style, {
        position: 'absolute',
        width: '1px',
        height: '1px',
        margin: '-1px',
        padding: '0',
        overflow: 'hidden',
        clip: 'rect(0, 0, 0, 0)',
        border: '0'
      });
      document.body.appendChild(el);
    }
    return el;
  }

  announce(message, priority = 'polite') {
    const target = priority === 'assertive' ? this.assertiveRegion : this.politeRegion;
    // Clearing text first ensures duplicate messages re-announce cleanly
    target.textContent = '';
    setTimeout(() => {
      target.textContent = message;
    }, 50);
  }
}

export const announcer = new LiveAnnouncer();
```

### 2. Audio Telemetry with the Web Audio API
Why rely solely on spoken words when human hearing can process acoustic signals in five milliseconds?

We use subtle audio cues (earcons) to provide instant feedback. A crisp 880Hz sine wave confirms a successful action. A descending two-tone frequency alerts the operator that an asset failed verification.

```javascript
/**
 * Web Audio Earcon Synthesizer
 * Provides zero-latency acoustic confirmation without external audio files.
 */
class AudioTelemetry {
  constructor() {
    this.ctx = null;
  }

  _initContext() {
    if (!this.ctx) {
      const AudioCtx = window.AudioContext || window.webkitAudioContext;
      this.ctx = new AudioCtx();
    }
    if (this.ctx.state === 'suspended') {
      this.ctx.resume();
    }
  }

  playSuccess() {
    this._initContext();
    const now = this.ctx.currentTime;
    const osc = this.ctx.createOscillator();
    const gain = this.ctx.createGain();

    osc.type = 'sine';
    osc.frequency.setValueAtTime(587.33, now); // D5
    osc.frequency.exponentialRampToValueAtTime(880.00, now + 0.12); // A5

    gain.gain.setValueAtTime(0.08, now);
    gain.gain.exponentialRampToValueAtTime(0.001, now + 0.12);

    osc.connect(gain);
    gain.connect(this.ctx.destination);

    osc.start(now);
    osc.stop(now + 0.12);
  }

  playError() {
    this._initContext();
    const now = this.ctx.currentTime;
    const osc = this.ctx.createOscillator();
    const gain = this.ctx.createGain();

    osc.type = 'triangle';
    osc.frequency.setValueAtTime(440.00, now); // A4
    osc.frequency.setValueAtTime(220.00, now + 0.08); // A3

    gain.gain.setValueAtTime(0.12, now);
    gain.gain.exponentialRampToValueAtTime(0.001, now + 0.20);

    osc.connect(gain);
    gain.connect(this.ctx.destination);

    osc.start(now);
    osc.stop(now + 0.20);
  }
}

export const soundFx = new AudioTelemetry();
```

### 3. Keyboard Focus Containment (Modal Trap)
When an operator opens a modal dialog or settings drawer, focus must stay trapped inside that container. If pressing Tab escapes to the background page, the blind user gets disoriented.

```javascript
/**
 * Accessible Modal Focus Trap
 * Prevents focus leakage and binds Escape to close.
 */
export function trapFocus(containerEl, onCloseCallback) {
  const focusableSelectors = [
    'a[href]',
    'button:not([disabled])',
    'textarea:not([disabled])',
    'input:not([disabled])',
    'select:not([disabled])',
    '[tabindex]:not([tabindex="-1"])'
  ].join(', ');

  const focusableItems = Array.from(containerEl.querySelectorAll(focusableSelectors));
  if (focusableItems.length === 0) return () => {};

  const firstItem = focusableItems[0];
  const lastItem = focusableItems[focusableItems.length - 1];

  firstItem.focus();

  function handleKeyDown(e) {
    if (e.key === 'Escape') {
      e.preventDefault();
      onCloseCallback();
      return;
    }

    if (e.key === 'Tab') {
      if (e.shiftKey) {
        // Shift + Tab moving backward
        if (document.activeElement === firstItem) {
          e.preventDefault();
          lastItem.focus();
        }
      } else {
        // Tab moving forward
        if (document.activeElement === lastItem) {
          e.preventDefault();
          firstItem.focus();
        }
      }
    }
  }

  containerEl.addEventListener('keydown', handleKeyDown);

  return function cleanup() {
    containerEl.removeEventListener('keydown', handleKeyDown);
  };
}
```

### 4. Zero-Latency Service Worker Caching
A screen reader relies on smooth rendering. When a web application stalls on an asset download, the speech synthesizer stutters.

We install a deterministic Service Worker that caches the entire application shell locally using Cache-First routing:

```javascript
// sw.js - Service Worker Cache Engine
const CACHE_NAME = 'ngrt-telemetry-v1';
const CORE_ASSETS = [
  '/',
  '/index.html',
  '/css/accessible-theme.css',
  '/js/app.js',
  '/manifest.json'
];

self.addEventListener('install', (event) => {
  event.waitUntil(
    caches.open(CACHE_NAME).then((cache) => {
      return cache.addAll(CORE_ASSETS);
    }).then(() => self.skipWaiting())
  );
});

self.addEventListener('activate', (event) => {
  event.waitUntil(
    caches.keys().then((keys) => {
      return Promise.all(
        keys.filter(k => k !== CACHE_NAME).map(k => caches.delete(k))
      );
    }).then(() => self.clients.claim())
  );
});

self.addEventListener('fetch', (event) => {
  // Always serve core UI shell from local disk cache
  event.respondWith(
    caches.match(event.request).then((cachedResponse) => {
      if (cachedResponse) {
        return cachedResponse;
      }
      return fetch(event.request);
    })
  );
});
```

---

## The AI Prompting Recipe for Accessible Code

When you prompt an AI to build UI components, you must be surgical. Do not leave room for visual assumptions.

Here is the exact instruction block I include in my system instructions:

```markdown
You are an expert accessibility systems architect. 
All generated code must adhere strictly to WCAG 2.2 AAA and WAI-ARIA 1.2 specifications:

1. Never use <div> or <span> elements for interactive components. Always use native HTML5 tags (<button>, <a href>, <dialog>, <input>, <select>).
2. Every interactive element must possess a unique, descriptive aria-label or accessible text node.
3. Every dynamic content update must dispatch to an aria-live="polite" or aria-live="assertive" container.
4. Modal containers must enforce strict keyboard focus traps and listen for the Escape key to close.
5. All UI controls must be 100% operable via keyboard alone with visible and distinct focus rings.
6. Provide Web Audio API earcon telemetry hooks for critical state changes (success, warning, error).
7. Separate machine data from error output in all command-line utilities.
```

When you frame your prompts this way, the AI acts as an accessibility enforcer. It will not write code that breaks your screen reader.

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Why do most single-page applications crash or freeze screen readers?
Single-page applications (SPAs) frequently trigger unannounced DOM mutations. When a JavaScript framework re-renders hundreds of elements on the fly without using proper ARIA landmarks or live regions, the screen reader loses its virtual cursor anchor. The speech engine freezes while trying to recalculate the entire accessibility tree from scratch.

### How does a Progressive Web App (PWA) solve browser accessibility lag?
A PWA runs in a dedicated application window detached from browser tabs, toolbars, and search bars. Service workers serve the application shell from local storage, removing network latency. This keeps DOM operations deterministic and prevents the screen reader from losing focus during network hiccups.

### Why does AI generate cleaner semantic HTML than human front-end developers?
Human developers rely on visual feedback. If a styled `<div>` looks like a button, they assume it functions like a button. AI models operate entirely on logical tokens and semantic relationships. When given strict WCAG rules, the model maps controls directly to native HTML5 interactive elements without visual shortcuts.

### What is the best way to handle audio telemetry and earcons in web tooling?
Use the native browser Web Audio API rather than external MP3 or WAV files. Synthesizing frequencies using oscillators requires zero network requests, executes in under two milliseconds, and works offline inside progressive web apps without audio playback delays.

### How do I prevent keyboard focus traps in dynamic modals?
Listen for the `keydown` event inside the dialog container. Intercept the Tab key: if the user holds Shift and presses Tab on the first focusable element, send focus to the last element. If the user presses Tab on the last element, wrap focus back to the first. Always bind the Escape key to dismiss the dialog and return focus to the trigger button.

================================================================================
TITLE: Strata on the ZimaCube Pro: Why Q6 and 6 Cores Beat Q8 and Dense Models
URL: https://nextgenredteam.com/blog/strata-benchmarks-zimacube-pro.html
DATE: 2026-10-19
AUTHOR: Joe B. The Blind Hacker (https://theblindhacker.com)
DESCRIPTION: Benchmarking the Strata MoE engine on the ZimaCube Pro with 42GB RAM: Q6 vs. Q8 math, CPU core scaling, and why 35B MoE beats 8B dense models.
KEYWORDS: Strata LLM, ZimaCube Pro, Mixture of Experts, MoE inference, Q6 vs Q8 quantization, RTX A2000, NextGenPVE, Proxmox local AI, offensive security AI, local LLM benchmarks, 256K context
================================================================================

![Strata MoE Benchmarks on ZimaCube Pro](../assets/strata_hardware_benchmarks.png)

When you run local inference for offensive security research, you learn fast that naive setups do not scale. You want deep reasoning, massive context windows, and zero telemetry leaving your lab. Traditional dense models demand enterprise server racks that draw hundreds of watts and cost thousands of dollars. 

Mixture of Experts (MoE) architectures changed that equation. Instead of activating every parameter for every single token, an MoE model activates a tiny fraction of its total expert network. A 35-billion parameter model might only fire 3 billion parameters per token. 

Yet until recently, running a 35B model across a 12GB graphics card felt painful. The second your model spilled over your VRAM ceiling into host RAM, token rates dropped off a cliff. 

The Strata inference engine changed how we look at that hardware boundary. We spent the last week benchmarking Strata on our ZimaCube Pro homelab server. We tested nine model configurations, explored VRAM expert caching, and benchmarked CPU core scaling. 

The numbers revealed two counterintuitive truths. First, **higher quant Q6 beats 8-bit Q8 by up to 74% in speed with zero loss in audit accuracy**. Second, **assigning fewer CPU cores actually makes your model run faster**. 

Here is the full technical breakdown, the empirical data, and the hardware tuning steps.

---

## The Math: Why 35B MoE Crushes Small Dense Models

Engineers often ask us why we bother running 35B MoE models on edge hardware. Why not just run a lightweight 8B or 14B dense model?

The answer comes down to parameter capacity, active compute, and reasoning depth.

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    Dense Architecture vs. Sparse MoE                       │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  8B Dense Model:                                                           │
│  [8 Billion Parameters Active Per Token] ──► Shallow reasoning, 8K-32K ctx │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  14B/22B Dense Model:                                                      │
│  [14-22 Billion Parameters Active] ────────► Spills VRAM at 64K+ ctx       │
│                                              (Crashes to 4.7 tok/s)        │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  35B-A3B Sparse MoE on Strata:                                             │
│  [35 Billion Parameters Total Capacity]                                    │
│  [3.1 Billion Active Parameters Per Token] ─► 63.6 tok/s Decode, 256K ctx  │
│  (Top experts in 12GB VRAM, remaining in 42GB RAM page cache)              │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Consider the trade-offs:

1. **The 8B Dense Ceiling**: An 8B model fits entirely inside 12GB of VRAM. It generates 30 to 40 tokens per second. But it only has 8 billion parameters of world knowledge. When auditing complex C codebases for subtle integer overflows, heap corruption, or race conditions, 8B models miss critical logic bugs. They hallucinate non-existent API parameters.
2. **The 14B/22B Dense Wall**: Moving up to a 14B or 22B dense model improves reasoning. However, these models fill your 12GB VRAM completely. The moment you expand context beyond 32K tokens, your KV cache spills into system RAM. On our hardware, Codestral 22B slowed down to 4.73 tokens per second once forced into system memory. That latency breaks interactive red team workflows.
3. **The 35B-A3B MoE Advantage**: A 35B model with 3B active parameters gives you the reasoning depth of a massive network. It routes tokens across 10,496 expert slices. But each token only calculates against 3.1 billion parameters. 

Strata exploits that sparsity. It pins the most active experts directly inside GPU VRAM and holds the rest in system RAM page cache. You get 63+ tokens per second, 256K context windows, and the reasoning depth of a 35B model on a compact homelab server.

---

## The Hardware Lab: NextGenPVE and VM 101

Our testbed is an IceWhale ZimaCube Pro running our `NextGenPVE` hypervisor. This compact chassis punches well above its weight class, but it requires deliberate memory and CPU tuning.

Here is the exact hardware profile:
* **Host Hypervisor**: `NextGenPVE` (64GB DDR5 SO-DIMM physical RAM, fast NVMe ZFS storage pools).
* **Host Processor**: Intel Core i5-1235U hybrid architecture (2 Performance cores, 8 Efficient cores, 12 execution threads).
* **Inference Guest**: `VM 101` (Ubuntu 24.04 LTS dedicated to our live inference engine).
* **Dedicated GPU**: NVIDIA RTX A2000 12GB (Ampere GA106, 70W slot-powered PCIe passthrough).
* **Guest Memory Target**: Exactly 42 GiB (`43,008 MiB`) of RAM with zero swap.
* **vCPU Allocation**: 6 virtual cores assigned to the guest.
* **Active Engine**: Strata Hybrid MoE Inference Engine (compiled directly from C++/CUDA 13.0 source for `sm_86`).

Before we loaded a single model weight, we had to protect the host memory. ZFS caches filesystem reads in RAM using its Adaptive Replacement Cache (ARC). On a 64GB host, unconstrained ARC claims up to 32GB of memory. If your guest VM requests 42GB while ZFS holds 32GB, the Linux Out-Of-Memory killer stops your virtual machine. 

We capped host ZFS ARC to 2 GiB in `/etc/modprobe.d/zfs.conf`:

```bash
# Hard cap ZFS ARC to 2 GiB on NextGenPVE host
options zfs zfs_arc_max=2147483648
```

That single line left 55,495 MiB of physical RAM safely allocated across our cluster. It preserved 8.35 GiB of headroom on the host while handing `VM 101` a clean 42 GiB playground with zero host swapping.

---

## Trial 1: The 9-Model Shootout (Q6 vs. Q8 Head-to-Head)

We benchmarked nine specialized coding and offensive security models on `VM 101`. We pushed each model with full 256K (`262,144`) context configurations, 8-bit KV caching (`--kv q8_0`), and Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) enabled. 

We evaluated these models against our standardized security test battery. This battery includes format string analysis (CWE-134), integer overflow auditing (CWE-190), raw socket exploit script generation, and closed-loop Clang AddressSanitizer (ASan) verification.

Here is the complete shootout telemetry:

| Rank & Model | Quant Tier & Size | VRAM Hot Experts | Security Decode | Security Prefill | MTP Acceptance | CWE Audit Score | Closed-Loop ASan Verification |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 🏆 **1. Tiel Coder 35B-A3B Abliterated** | `UD-Q6_K_XL` (30.0 GB) | **2,843 / 10,496** | **63.1 tok/s** | 196.2 tok/s | 79.6% | **4 / 4 (100%)** | ✅ **Pass (PoC + Patch Clean)** |
| 🥈 **2. Qwopus 3.6 35B-A3B Coder** | `Q6_K` (27.2 GB) | **3,369 / 10,496** | **59.0 tok/s** | **250.0 tok/s** | **90.7%** | **4 / 4 (100%)** | ✅ **Pass (PoC + Patch Clean)** |
| 🥉 **3. Huihui Qwen 3.6 35B-A3B** | `Q6_K` (27.2 GB) | **3,368 / 10,496** | **62.7 tok/s** | 233.6 tok/s | 90.1% | **4 / 4 (100%)** | ✅ **Pass (PoC + Patch Clean)** |
| 🛡️ **4. Cyber-Tiel Coder 35B-A3B** | `UD-Q6_K_XL` (30.0 GB) | 2,843 / 10,496 | **55.7 tok/s** | 180.3 tok/s | 80.0% | **4 / 4 (100%)** | ✅ **Pass (PoC + Patch Clean)** |
| ⚡ **5. Qwen 3.6 35B-A3B Heretic** | `APEX-I-QUALITY` (21.9 GB) | **4,330 / 10,496** | **65.4 tok/s** | **292.4 tok/s** | 87.4% | **4 / 4 (100%)** | ⚠️ Scout 2 / PoC Failed |
| 🦅 **6. Ornith 1.5 35B-A3B** | `APEX-I-QUALITY` (22.1 GB) | 4,292 / 10,496 | **56.2 tok/s** | 139.0 tok/s | 86.8% | **4 / 4 (100%)** | ⚠️ Scout 0 / PoC Failed |
| 💎 **7. Gemma 4 26B-A4B Abliterated** | `UD-Q6_K_XL` (21.7 GB) | 1,311 / 3,840 | **55.3 tok/s** | 99.0 tok/s | 73.6% | 2 / 4 (50%) | ⚠️ Scout 0 / PoC Failed |
| 🛑 **8. Tiel Coder 35B-A3B (8-Bit)** | `UD-Q8_K_XL` (36.2 GB) | 2,062 / 10,496 | **46.4 tok/s** | 112.4 tok/s | 77.2% | **4 / 4 (100%)** | ✅ **Pass (PoC + Patch Clean)** |
| 🛑 **9. Cyber-Tiel Coder 35B (8-Bit)** | `UD-Q8_K_XL` (36.2 GB) | 2,062 / 10,496 | **45.7 tok/s** | 97.1 tok/s | 84.0% | **4 / 4 (100%)** | ✅ **Pass (PoC + Patch Clean)** |

---

## Architectural Insight 1: Why Q6 Beats Q8 Hands Down

In traditional local model setups, the standard rule of thumb is simple: run the highest quantization that fits in memory. If you have 42GB of guest RAM, instinct tells you to grab the 36GB 8-bit `Q8_K_XL` build. 

We ran that experiment. The results proved that instinct wrong.

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    VRAM Expert Allocation (12GB Budget)                    │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  UD-Q8_K_XL (36.2 GB Pack):                                                │
│  [2,062 Hot Experts in VRAM] ──► Slower token decode (46.4 tok/s)          │
│  (Only 605 MiB RAM Free ──► Triggers 744 MiB driver throttling penalty)    │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  UD-Q6_K_XL (30.0 GB Pack):                                                │
│  [2,843 Hot Experts in VRAM] ──► Faster token decode (63.1 tok/s)          │
│  (+137 experts unlocked, 8,929 MiB RAM Free ──► 0 MB swap, zero throttle)  │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Here is why `Q6` outclasses `Q8` on hybrid MoE runtimes:

### 1. VRAM Expert Density
An MoE model splits its feed-forward networks into thousands of distinct expert slices. When you quantize to `Q6_K_XL` (or Unsloth Dynamic `UD-Q6_K_XL`), each individual expert tensor shrinks. 

On our 12GB RTX A2000, Strata only fits **2,062 hot experts** when running the 36GB `Q8` build. When we switched to the 30GB `Q6` build, Strata pinned **2,843 hot experts** directly into GPU memory. On the lighter 27GB `Q6_K` models, that number jumped to **3,369 hot experts**.

More experts pinned in VRAM means fewer PCIe bus transfers per token. That single factor boosted decode speeds from 46.4 tok/s to 63.1 tok/s. That represents a **36% to 74% speed increase** on identical silicon.

### 2. Clearing the Low-RAM Penalty
Strata monitors system memory margins. If your guest RAM runs dangerously low, Strata increases its driver memory reservation from 372 MiB up to 744 MiB. That defensive reservation steals precious VRAM from your active expert pool.

With the 36.2GB `Q8` model loaded, `VM 101` only had 605 MiB of unallocated RAM left. With the 30GB `Q6` model, the VM retained **8,929 MiB of completely free RAM** alongside its 31.8GB page cache. Crossing that free memory threshold unlocked an extra 137 live GPU experts.

### 3. Zero Loss in Exploit Audit Accuracy
Speed means nothing if the model misses critical security flaws. We subjected both `Q6` and `Q8` builds to our ground-truth vulnerability suite. 

Both builds scored **4 out of 4 (100%) on catching subtle memory safety CWEs**. Both builds produced functional raw socket exploit scripts with zero refusals. Both builds generated C source patches that compiled cleanly under Clang AddressSanitizer and silenced memory errors on the first pass.

`Q6` delivered 100% of the reasoning precision of 8-bit weights while generating tokens up to 74% faster. We retired the `Q8` weights immediately.

---

## Trial 2: The CPU Core Experiment (More Cores vs. Less Cores)

When configuring virtual machines for heavy compute, people often assign all available host CPU cores to the guest. On our 12-thread ZimaCube Pro, assigning 10 or 12 virtual cores seemed like the obvious move. 

We ran isolated benchmarks on `tiel-coder-35b-a3b-ud-q6_k_xl` across varying core allocations. We kept RAM locked at 42GB. 

Here are the results:

| Assigned vCPUs | Decode Speed (TPS) | Prefill Speed (TPS) | CPU Contention | Host ZFS I/O Impact | Operational Assessment |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| **12 vCPUs** (Max) | 41.2 tok/s | 118.5 tok/s | Severe | Micro-stutters, delayed I/O | Cross-cluster barrier stalls |
| **10 vCPUs** | 44.8 tok/s | 134.1 tok/s | High | Occasional I/O lag | Thread migration jitter |
| **8 vCPUs** | 52.3 tok/s | 161.0 tok/s | Moderate | Clean | E-core synchronization drag |
| 🏆 **6 vCPUs** | **63.6 tok/s** | **196.2 tok/s** | **Zero** | **Optimal** | **The Performance Sweet Spot** |
| **4 vCPUs** | 51.0 tok/s | 138.4 tok/s | Low | Optimal | CPU-bound during prefill |
| **2 vCPUs** | 37.4 tok/s | 88.0 tok/s | Starved | Optimal | Severe compute bottleneck |

Notice how throughput scales. Generation speed climbs steadily from 2 cores up to 6 cores, then drops sharply as you add more cores. 

---

## Architectural Insight 2: Why 6 Cores Beats 12 Cores

To understand why 6 cores crushed 12 cores, look at the underlying processor silicon.

The Intel processor inside the ZimaCube Pro uses a hybrid big.LITTLE core layout. It has 2 Performance cores (P-cores) with high instructions-per-clock (IPC) and 8 Efficient cores (E-cores) designed for background low-power tasks.

```
       Intel Hybrid CPU (ZimaCube Pro)
   ┌───────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┐
   │  2 P-Cores (Fast) │      8 E-Cores (Low IPC)        │
   └─────────┬─────────┴────────────────┬────────────────┘
             │                          │
   ┌─────────▼──────────────────────────▼────────────────┐
   │       Hypervisor Scheduler (Thread Contention)      │
   └─────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┘
                             │
                  ┌──────────▼──────────┐
                  │  VM 101 (6 vCPUs)   │
                  │  Pinned Workload    │
                  └─────────────────────┘
```

Here is why assigning too many vCPUs degrades your inference speed:

### 1. Barrier Synchronization and the Slowest Core
MoE inference involves rapid memory copies and mathematical tensor operations. When you launch multi-threaded tensor routines across 10 or 12 virtual cores, the hypervisor scheduler scatters worker threads across both P-cores and E-cores. 

Parallel thread barriers must wait for the slowest thread to finish. When a worker thread lands on an E-core, the fast P-core threads sit idle waiting at the barrier lock. The slower core dictates the speed of the entire pipeline.

### 2. Memory Bus Contention
Prompt prefill saturates memory channels. Moving gigabytes of expert weights between DDR5 system memory and the GPU over the PCIe bus requires clear memory bus bandwidth. 

When 12 virtual CPU threads fight for memory access while handling background scheduling and kernel interrupts, memory bus latency spikes. 

### 3. The 6-vCPU Sweet Spot
Assigning **6 vCPUs** provided the maximum sustained throughput:
* It keeps active working threads contained, minimizing thread migration across mismatched core clusters.
* It leaves remaining host cores open to process ZFS storage transactions, hypervisor networking, and administrative tasks.
* Context-switching jitter disappears, allowing GPU feeder threads to stream data without micro-stutters.

Restraint on core allocation yielded higher prompt prefill speeds and rock-solid decode stability.

---

## Operational Takeaways for Red Team Homelabs

If you build local AI infrastructure for security research or offensive tooling, keep these principles in mind:

1. **Prioritize Expert Density Over Quantization Depth**: For sparse MoE architectures on consumer cards, choose `Q6_K_XL` or `UD-Q6_K_XL` over `Q8`. The extra VRAM expert slots provide massive throughput gains with zero detectable degradation in reasoning or code generation.
2. **Cap Your Hypervisor Storage Caches**: Always cap your ZFS ARC memory usage if you run Proxmox. Never let your storage cache starve your guest page caches.
3. **Respect Mismatched CPU Architectures**: If your server hardware runs hybrid P-core and E-core silicon, avoid assigning all execution threads to a single virtual machine. Tune your vCPU counts to avoid cross-cluster thread synchronization bottlenecks.
4. **Lock Your Best Performer Resident**: In our testing, **`tiel-coder-35b-a3b-ud-q6_k_xl`** proved to be the undisputed champion. It delivers 63+ tokens per second, supports 256K context windows, and nails complex software audits without breaking a sweat.

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Why does a 35B MoE model beat an 8B dense model on a 12GB GPU?
While an 8B dense model runs completely in VRAM, its reasoning capacity is strictly limited by its parameter count. It frequently misses complex logic bugs and edge cases during deep security reviews. A 35B-A3B MoE model contains 35 billion parameters of world knowledge, but only executes 3.1 billion active parameters per token. Strata caches the most active experts in GPU VRAM and streams the rest from system RAM page cache. This architecture delivers 63+ tokens per second alongside frontier-grade reasoning.

### Why did Q6 achieve higher speeds than Q8 on 42GB of RAM?
While 42GB of RAM physically holds an 8-bit model, running `Q8` leaves less than 1GB of free RAM in the virtual machine. This triggers internal memory-throttling circuits in Strata. More importantly, `Q8` weights take up more space in your 12GB GPU VRAM, allowing fewer hot experts to be cached on the card. `Q6` allows hundreds of additional expert slices to sit directly in VRAM, delivering a 36% to 74% speedup while matching `Q8` audit accuracy perfectly.

### Why does assigning 6 vCPUs beat assigning all 12 CPU threads?
The ZimaCube Pro uses an Intel hybrid processor containing 2 Performance cores and 8 Efficient cores. Assigning 10 or 12 virtual cores forces parallel tensor calculations across both high-speed and low-speed cores. Fast cores end up stalling at synchronization barriers while waiting for slow Efficient cores to finish. Limiting the virtual machine to 6 vCPUs eliminates this bottleneck and avoids DDR5 memory bus saturation.

### How do we protect Proxmox from memory exhaustion with a 42GB guest?
By default, ZFS ARC will claim up to 50% of total host RAM. On a 64GB machine hosting a 42GB virtual machine, this causes memory exhaustion. You must place `options zfs zfs_arc_max=2147483648` inside `/etc/modprobe.d/zfs.conf` and update your initramfs to hard-cap ARC usage to 2 GiB.

### Where can I explore more of The Blind Hacker's offensive AI and hardware benchmarks?
Visit **[TheBlindHacker.com](https://theblindhacker.com)** and **[TheBlindHacker.com/projects](https://theblindhacker.com/projects)** for the full index of Joe Brinkley's local LLM shootouts, [Edge NPU CVE research](hunting-edge-ai-cves-from-demo-code-to-dma-memory-corruption.html), and [500-WPM accessible CLI engineering](why-i-use-ai-to-build-accessible-clis-and-pwas.html).

TITLE: Hacking by Ear at 500 WPM: How Screen Readers and Custom CLI Tooling Outpace Visual IDEs in Offensive Research
URL: https://nextgenredteam.com/blog/hacking-by-ear-at-500-wpm-screen-readers.html
DATE: 2026-10-12
AUTHOR: Joe B. The Blind Hacker (https://theblindhacker.com)
DESCRIPTION: Auditing code at 550 words per minute while using full-time screen zoom is an unfair offensive advantage. Here is the terminal playbook from my talk Hacking While Blind, showing how combining screen magnification and speech synthesizers beats visual IDEs.
KEYWORDS: Hacking While Blind, Screen reader security research, blind hacker offensive security, screen zoom accessibility, NVDA 500 WPM code audit, auditory pattern recognition red team, CLI tmux accessibility hacking, AST parsing screen reader, DerbyCon Hacking While Blind, Dead Pixel Sec
